opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was back in my PhD days, and recommender systems were kind of the hot thing at the time; a lot of people were working on them. But the experiments always felt a little strange to me. A lot of it came down to the datasets and the evaluation setup. You'd have these user-item interaction datasets, and the "modeling" was often about squeezing out a small gain on some ranking metric, like hit rate or NDCG, on a benchmark that may or may not reflect anything real. Whether a method worked often depended on how you sampled negatives, how you split the data, or which baselines you tuned properly. So it never felt like you were learning something fundamental about the model.

I also didn't find it very intellectually satisfying. With language, you can look at the outputs and reason about what the model is doing. You get a feel for whether it's understanding something. With recsys, you're staring at IDs and embeddings, and the signal is so noisy and so tied to the specific dataset that it was hard to build intuition. You'd get a number go up and you wouldn't really know why, or whether it would hold anywhere else.

So over time I gravitated toward language and more general modeling problems, where the progress felt more real and more transferable. That's ultimately what pulled me toward working on Transformers and language models.

r001.rationale: The response explains that recommender-system experiments felt strange because noisy, dataset-dependent results made it hard to build intuition or understand why a model improved, unlike language modeling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was back during my PhD, and also a bit at Google early on — I did a fair amount of work on recommender systems, like deep learning for recsys, collaborative filtering, that kind of thing. And the thing that made it feel strange was that the experiments never really felt like they were measuring anything real. You'd be working with these benchmark datasets — MovieLens, Netflix, whatever — and the evaluation protocols were just all over the place. Everyone would sample negatives differently, use different splits, and you could basically get whatever result you wanted depending on how you set it up. So you'd get a 2% improvement on some metric and you'd genuinely have no idea whether it meant anything.

And the other part was that the models themselves were kind of unsatisfying to work on. In recsys, so much of the actual signal lives in the data and the features and the serving pipeline, not in the architecture. So you'd spend all this time designing some fancy attention mechanism over user histories, and then in practice a well-tuned matrix factorization baseline would do just as well, or better. It felt like you were iterating in this little sandbox that was disconnected from the actual problem.

Compare that to language modeling, where you train a model, you see loss go down, you scale it up, and there's this very clear, almost physical sense that something is happening — the model is getting better at a thing you can actually see. There's a kind of ground truth there. With recsys experiments I just never had that feeling. It was a lot of noise, a lot of tuning, and not much of the joy you get from watching a model actually learn. So at some point I just decided I'd rather work on the stuff where the signal was clearer, and that pulled me toward language.

r001.rationale: The response explains that recommender-system results depended heavily on inconsistent evaluation choices and data or serving details, while elaborate architectures could lose to matrix factorization. This conveys that ordinary intuitions about modeling did not hold in that setting.

astra-6.text: What I found strange was that a lot of the work was about ranking items using user IDs and item IDs. You’d change the architecture, run an experiment, and get a slightly better number, but it was hard to develop an intuition for why it worked. I didn’t find that feedback loop very satisfying. With language, I could look at the inputs and outputs, understand what the model was getting wrong, and connect the experiment to something meaningful. That was much more enjoyable to me.

r001.rationale: He says the experiments made it hard to develop an intuition for why changes worked, communicating that his usual modeling intuitions did not hold in recommender systems.

sol-6.1.text: What I found strange was how difficult it was to tell whether a modeling idea was actually better. You could change the negative sampling, the data split, or the evaluation setup, and the results would move around. So you might spend a lot of time tuning something without feeling that you’d learned much about the model itself. I enjoyed the part where you come up with an idea and try to understand why it works, and those experiments didn’t always give me that satisfaction.

r001.rationale: The response says results varied with negative sampling, data splits, and evaluation setup, making it hard to tell what was better. It does not say that Yi Tay’s usual modeling intuitions failed to hold.
